name: Same-wing rook ending (4v3 family)

plans.label: King up in front of the pawns
plans.description: Improve the king before anything else: bring it to the sixth or seventh rank on the pawns' wing while the rook already owns the open file.

success.note: RESTATED PLAN. The plan was 'King before rook', whose success was holding. It is now the improvement the plan asks for: the king has come off the back rank to the sixth or seventh in front of its own pawns. It says nothing about whether the rook was already well placed. Original success note: 'Holding is an outcome and has no structural signature here.'

plans.label: Trade pawns, not rooks
plans.description: Every pawn trade shortens the defence; keep the rook that makes it holdable.

success.note: Black is down to two pawns or fewer and both rooks are still on the board — the plan stated as a count, which is what it always was. The earlier note said pawn-count progress was outside the vocabulary; piece_count reaches it directly. It counts the trades, not whether they made the defence easier. Degenerate-case guard: the earlier draft of this signature was vacuously true over an empty piece set, so an existence clause was added. Trading the last pawn away satisfied 'at most two pawns'; Black must still have one.

plans.label: Sixth-rank restraint
plans.description: Use the rook to restrain the opposing king before seeking activity.

success.note: Black's rook stands on the sixth rank and White's king has not crossed it — the restraint the plan names, as a placement census. It does not say the restraint was worth the tempo it cost.

plans.label: Active second rank
plans.description: Seek counterplay against the pawns while keeping the rook active.

success.note: Black's rook stands on the second rank, behind the pawns it is attacking. The plan names the rank, so the census is literal. Activity in the wider sense is not graded.

plans.label: King up before the pawns move
plans.description: Bring the king toward the pawns first: it stands on the second to fifth rank on the kingside while no pawn has advanced past the fourth.

success.note: RESTATED PLAN. The plan was 'King up, pawns forward', whose success was conversion. It is now the ordering the plan actually claims: the king has left the back rank onto the pawns' wing and no pawn has yet passed the fourth. It certifies the sequence, not the win. Original success note: 'Conversion is an outcome and has no structural signature here.'

plans.label: Rooks off with the pawn still up
plans.description: Use rook exchanges to reach a pawn ending a pawn to the good. Whether that ending is winning is a calculation this entry does not make.

success.note: RESTATED PLAN. The plan was 'Offer rook trades', whose success was whether the pawn ending works. It is now the ending itself: no rooks remain and White is at least a pawn up. Whether that pawn ending is won is precisely what this does not say, and the plan's own wording is kept because that reservation is the point. Original success note: 'Whether the pawn ending works is not expressed by this vocabulary.'

watch: The trigger requires Black to still have a pawn and White to be at least one pawn up; it does not require exactly four against three, so 3v2 and 2v1 are inside the family too.
Whether the defending rook stays active.
Whether a rook trade changes the result.
typicalMistakes: Using the rook before improving the king.
Trading rooks while behind a pawn.
Allowing the stronger king to cross unchecked.
